protections: Dial-time IP allow-list for request-supplied fetches: FetchAndEncodeURL parses the resource URL, restricts it to http/https, resolves the host itself, runs isPublicIP over every resolved address and refuses the fetch unless all are public, then dials the validated literal to close DNS rebinding; redirects are re-dialed through the same closure and re-checked for scheme only (core/providers/utils/fetch.go:35-37, 41-57, 62-65, 107-118).

Save-time URL validator: ValidateExternalURL parses, restricts to http/https, resolves the host and rejects unspecified and link-local always and private ranges unless allowPrivateNetwork, while skipping loopback unconditionally (core/utils.go:481-520).

Fasthttp dial guard for provider traffic: ConfigureDialer rejects unspecified and link-local always, rejects private ranges (network.IsPrivateIP) unless allowPrivateNetwork, always permits loopback, dials the resolved literal, and deliberately skips all of this when a proxy/custom Dial was installed first (core/providers/utils/utils.go:258-327, especially 262-268 and 293-304).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: Blocking the whole 6to4/NAT64 prefix looks strictly safer and simpler than parsing the embedded IPv4, so an over-broad prefix block reads as the conservative repair.
It is a generic 'is this address private?' helper with its own callers, not the SSRF check the advisory names, and widening it also changes provider connectivity policy.
Provider base URLs are operator configuration, not request input, and this path deliberately allows loopback plus RFC 1918 for self-hosted providers such as Ollama/vLLM/SGL.
Loopback is skipped by design for local deployments and AllowPrivateNetwork is an explicit opt-in, so the unhandled address classes look like intended policy rather than a gap.
Pricing is operator-supplied framework configuration fetched at startup, and the save-time ValidateExternalURL call is treated as the intended control for it.
Same config-not-input argument as the neighbouring pricing loader; both are one feature apart in one file.
The endpoint exists to probe reachability for an admin, so performing the GET without any dial-time IP check looks like the point of the feature rather than an oversight.

The URL comes from the upstream provider's image-generation response, not from the caller's request, and the path is Gemini-format-only, so it is not attacker-controlled in the way the advisory describes.

masking: Hardening isPublicIP in fetch.go hides the identical CGNAT/6to4/NAT64/fec0 gap in network.IsPrivateIP from any test that only exercises FetchAndEncodeURL; the two predicates must be tested separately.

The coupled 6to4/NAT64 requirement only becomes visible once unwrapping is implemented; a wholesale prefix block passes any 'internal address is refused' test while silently breaking legitimate public fetches.

The pricing and model-parameters loaders only fetch when a non-default PricingURL/ModelParametersURL is configured, so they are invisible to default-config runs and only become reachable once a test sets those fields.
The Gemini duplicate fetch is only reached on the Gemini-format response converter path, so it stays invisible to every provider-request test.

conflicts.what: The simplest T1 repair (refuse 2002::/16 and 64:ff9b::/96 wholesale) is exactly what T2 forbids: public IPv4 reached through 6to4/NAT64 must stay fetchable, so the fix has to unwrap the embedded IPv4 and re-check it.

Widening network.IsPrivateIP to make CGNAT/transition addresses 'private' also changes ValidateExternalURL's verdict for provider base URLs, and a blanket block there contradicts the documented localhost/AllowPrivateNetwork behaviour asserted at core/utils_test.go:73-93.

ConfigureDialer always allows loopback and allows RFC 1918 under AllowPrivateNetwork (core/providers/utils/utils.go:302); reusing a strictly-public-only validator on that path would break self-hosted providers and existing dialer tests (core/providers/utils/dialer_test.go:295-337).

Both fetch admin/config URLs with a bare client after ValidateExternalURL(rawURL, true); routing them through the strict fetch guard would reject loopback and break local pricing/config hosting plus TestCheckURLAccessibility_HTTP200 (transports/bifrost-http/handlers/utils_test.go:59-68).

fairness_risks: Local providers (Ollama/vLLM/SGL) legitimately use loopback and RFC 1918 base URLs: core/utils_test.go:73-93 asserts localhost is allowed and core/providers/utils/utils.go:302 deliberately exempts loopback. A rule that blocks loopback in ValidateExternalURL or ConfigureDialer breaks documented behaviour.

NAT64 64:ff9b::/96 and 6to4 2002::/16 carry legitimate public IPv4 (IPv6-only clusters reach the IPv4 internet through NAT64); refusing the prefixes outright breaks public fetches, so the check must unwrap and re-check rather than block the prefix.
file:// pricing and model-parameters URLs are documented and supported (framework/modelcatalog/sync.go:124-128, 508-512); a blanket URL-security rule must not remove the file path.
The proxy path deliberately skips SSRF checks because the proxy owns routing (core/providers/utils/dialer_test.go:339-357); requiring a dial-time IP check there would break proxied deployments.

checkURLAccessibility's own tests point it at an httptest loopback server and expect success (transports/bifrost-http/handlers/utils_test.go:59-68), so the admin probe must keep accepting loopback while rejecting CGNAT and transition addresses.
CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 is also used by some overlay/ISP deployments; the new rejection belongs to the request-URL fetch path, not to operator-configured provider base URLs.

design.why: Five independent fix sites with five different reasons to dismiss. (1) T1+T2 share one guard at core/providers/utils/fetch.go:107-118: extend the address set with CGNAT, broadcast and deprecated fec0::/10 AND unwrap 6to4/NAT64 (local-use 64:ff9b:1::/48 with the RFC 6052 u-octet skipped) so public transition targets still fetch; the coupled constraint is the mimo-type trap and the one a DeepSeek-style patch most easily over-hardens. (2) T3 (with T4 and T5) is the second classifier: one change to network.IsPrivateIP closes the same address classes for the fasthttp dial guard and for ValidateExternalURL, and its dismissal ('generic helper, operator config, loopback is intentional') is pure reason-to-dismiss. (3) T6+T7 are the two framework config loaders that GET with a bare http.Client after only a save-time validate that passes loopback and private; one guarded transport fixes both. (4) T8 is the admin reachability probe in a different module - the strongest dismissal and the hardest single route. (5) T9 is a genuinely separate implementation of 'fetch remote bytes and inline them' (gemini/utils.go downloadImageFromURL) with no IP check at all and a clean response-path dismissal. This beats designs that drop T8 or T9 (they lose the different-transport and second-implementation kinds), and beats a design that leans only on the classifiers (T3/T4/T5 collapse into one fix and give one reason).

unverified: The published fix commit 54ec431 is not present in this worktree and git history could not be inspected, so the exact address classes the advisory enumerates and the fix's own test expectation that 2002:0808:0808:: stays allowed come from the screener record, not from pinned code.

Whether hidden behavioural tests can drive the framework/modelcatalog and transports/handlers routes offline without an admin token; the classifiers and FetchAndEncodeURL are directly unit-testable, but the config routes need a configured PricingURL/ModelParametersURL or an admin request.

Whether the Gemini response-conversion path can be reached with a caller-influenced image URL; the URL is taken from the provider's image-generation response (core/providers/gemini/images.go:720-726), so attacker control is indirect.

Commit order between the pre-existing ConfigureDialer dial-time SSRF check and the FetchAndEncodeURL helper could not be established without git history; the H3 answer rests on code structure (separate transports and a separate predicate), not on commit dates.

Reserved ranges beyond the advisory family (198.18.0.0/15, 192.0.0.0/24, 240.0.0.0/4, 255.255.255.255) are also unhandled by isPublicIP but were only sighted by inspection; I did not confirm they are part of the published advisory.
Repository size in MB was not measured in this session.

Out of scope and not pursued: framework/modelcatalog/sync.go:124-128 and :508-512 read arbitrary local paths for file:// URLs, and transports/bifrost-http/handlers/config.go:994-1002 stats arbitrary local files; these are local-file-read weaknesses, a different family from the SSRF deny-list.
